questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A causal question dressed as a comparison
questions.learningObjective: identify why a treated-against-control comparison is not yet a causal answer
questions.stem: A clinic asks whether a nightly medication shortens recovery. The report reads that patients who take it recover in 6 days on average and patients who do not take it recover in 9. Why is that comparison not yet a causal answer?

options.text: The two groups differed before the medication began, so the comparison mixes the drug's effect with who chose to take it
The two averages came from different numbers of patients, so the gap is an artefact of the sample sizes
options.misconception: explains a difference in means by group size alone

options.text: Recovery time was never recorded by the study, so the comparison is not measuring the outcome it names
options.misconception: denies that the reported quantity was in fact recorded

options.text: The comparison is causal, since the patients who take a nightly medication are the ones who chose to recover
options.misconception: assumes choosing to take a medicine proves it caused the recovery

questions.explanation: Nobody is assigned to take this medication at random, and the people who take it differ before they start: they may be more worried, more healthy, or better able to follow a nightly routine. The nine-day figure is then the average outcome of people who did not take it, which is not the same quantity as the average outcome these particular takers would have had, so the three-day gap is a mixture of the drug and of the choosing. That mixture is what an adjustment or a design has to remove, and until it is removed the gap is a description of two populations rather than an estimate of what the drug does.
questions.hint: Ask what the takers looked like before the medication started.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A unit's two potential outcomes
questions.learningObjective: state what the potential outcomes framework says about one unit's effect
questions.stem: In the potential outcomes framework every unit has an outcome if it is treated and an outcome if it is not. What does the framework say the treatment effect is for one particular unit?

options.text: The difference between that unit's two outcomes, of which only one of them will ever actually be observed
The difference between the treated group's average outcome and the control group's average outcome
options.misconception: substitutes a group contrast for a single unit's two outcomes

options.text: The outcome the unit would have had under treatment, which the framework treats as known for every unit
options.misconception: claims both potential outcomes are known for every unit

options.text: Unobservable for every unit in the study, including the ones that were actually assigned to treatment
options.misconception: extends the unobservability claim to the units that were treated

questions.explanation: Each unit carries two potential outcomes fixed before assignment, and the effect for that unit is the difference between them, which is why the framework calls the missing half the fundamental problem of causal inference: for a treated unit you observe the treated outcome and never the untreated one, and for a control unit the reverse. An estimate is therefore always a claim about the average of those per-unit differences across a population, never a readout of any unit's own effect, and a policy that treats one person's response as the group average is making exactly that error. The framework's discipline is to state the target this way before looking at data, because the two halves being unobserved together is what forces a design rather than an adjustment to carry the argument.
questions.hint: Ask which of the unit's two outcomes the study can ever see.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the unobserved outcome must be a fact
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a counterfactual a quantity rather than a model output
questions.stem: The framework holds that each unit's outcome under the treatment it did not receive is a real quantity settled before assignment. Why does the framework insist on that?

options.text: The counterfactual is what the estimate is aiming at, so it has to be a fact about the unit rather than a model output
The counterfactual is directly measurable, so any estimate that skips it is incomplete by definition
options.misconception: believes the missing outcome can simply be read off the data

options.text: Saying it is settled in advance is the same as assuming the treatment does not affect the outcome
options.misconception: reads a definitional statement about timing as a null effect

options.text: Outcomes are random variables, so only their averages exist and per-unit quantities are not well defined
options.misconception: argues that per-unit quantities cannot be defined at all

questions.explanation: Saying the outcome was fixed before assignment is a statement about what the causal question means, not a claim that anyone can see it: the person had a definite recovery time awaiting them, and the treatment either delivered it or did not. That is what makes the target of an estimate a property of the world rather than of a fitted curve, and it is why the same data can be used to defend different causal claims depending on what the counterfactual is taken to be. The framework's price is that the counterfactual stays unobserved, so the work of causal inference shifts from measuring it to arranging circumstances in which the comparison stands in for it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the counterfactual is a fact about the world or a number a method produced.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What random assignment balances
questions.learningObjective: state what randomisation balances and how exactly
questions.stem: A trial sends 500 units to treatment and 500 to control by a coin flip of known probability. What does the randomisation itself balance, and what does it not guarantee?

options.text: Measured and unmeasured characteristics on average across the two arms, but not exactly in any single realisation
Every characteristic exactly in this particular trial, since a fair coin produces identical arms
options.misconception: believes a fair coin delivers exact balance in one realisation

options.text: Only the characteristics recorded before assignment, leaving everything else to chance
options.misconception: believes unmeasured characteristics are excluded by randomisation

options.text: Nothing at all, since balance has to be produced by matching units rather than by chance
options.misconception: believes matching is the only route to comparable groups

questions.explanation: Randomisation cannot control which units land where, so in any one trial an arm can come out lopsided on age or on prior severity by nothing more than luck; what it guarantees is that such lopsidedness has no systematic direction, so it washes out in expectation and shrinks as the trial grows. That is why an unadjusted difference between the arms is an unbiased estimate of the effect and why the balance table is a check on the draw rather than the source of the estimate. The sentence to avoid is the one reporting a table of small differences as proof that the trial worked, since a table that happens to look balanced is not what makes it balanced.
questions.hint: Ask what a coin flip controls, and what it merely makes more likely to cancel out.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The estimated effect from two arm means
questions.learningObjective: compute a difference in means as an effect estimate
questions.stem: Two hundred units are assigned to treatment and average 13.4 on the outcome; two hundred are assigned to control and average 9.1. What is the estimated effect of the treatment on the outcome?
questions.explanation: The estimate is 13.4 minus 9.1, which is 4.3, and the second route through the raw totals gives the same number: the treated units sum to 2680 and the control units to 1820, and dividing both by 200 returns 13.4 and 9.1 before the subtraction. Reporting 1.47 divides the two means and describes a ratio rather than a difference, and 47 per cent is that ratio expressed as a proportional change, which answers a different question and would mislead anyone who needs the size of the change itself. A single number is not the end of the answer, since the uncertainty around 4.3 is what says whether it is worth acting on.
questions.hint: Subtract the two averages, and check by dividing each average by nothing at all first.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Averaging four individual effects
questions.learningObjective: compute an average effect from a potential outcome table
questions.stem: For four units the framework records both outcomes. Unit 1 has 10 treated and 6 untreated, unit 2 has 14 and 12, unit 3 has 9 and 15, unit 4 has 18 and 16. What is the average of the four individual effects?
questions.explanation: The four effects are 4, 2, minus 6 and 2, which sum to 2 and average 0.5; the same figure falls out of the two columns, since the treated mean is 12.75 and the untreated mean 12.25. That the two routes agree is the point of the calculation, because the average of the differences is exactly the difference of the averages and would not be if the units were weighted unevenly. Unit 3 is the one worth pausing on, since a negative effect there is a unit harmed rather than helped, and an average of 0.5 conceals it completely, which is the argument for reporting the spread of individual effects as well as their centre.
questions.hint: Subtract within each unit first, then average; the columns must give the same answer.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A risk difference from two event counts
questions.learningObjective: compute a risk difference from event counts
questions.stem: Among 100 treated units, 20 have the outcome of interest, and among 100 control units, 8 have it. What is the risk difference between the groups?
questions.explanation: The risks are 20 over 100 and 8 over 100, so the difference is 0.20 minus 0.08, which is 0.12, and the second route (20 minus 8) over 100 gives the same 0.12. The 2.5 that divides the two risks is a ratio rather than a difference, and the two are not interchangeable: a ratio of 2.5 is consistent with risks of 0.20 against 0.08 and with 0.04 against 0.016, which are very different situations for a decision. When the outcome is rare, as it usually is in a trial, the difference and the ratio come close, and it is the rare case where quoting the ratio as though it were a difference understates the number of people affected.
questions.hint: Convert each count to a rate on its own group, then subtract the rates.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A balance table from a randomised trial
questions.learningObjective: interpret a randomisation balance table
questions.stem: A randomised trial reports shares of units in each arm: under 30 years 0.31 against 0.30, at least 60 years 0.28 against 0.31, prior outcome 0.44 against 0.45. What do these figures support?

options.text: The arms are close on the measured characteristics, which is what randomisation is expected to deliver in a sample
The arms are identical in this trial, since random assignment guarantees that every characteristic matches
options.misconception: reads a near-match as an exact match

options.text: The trial failed, since three characteristics showing any gap means the randomisation did not take
options.misconception: treats small sampling gaps as evidence of a broken assignment

options.text: The arms are balanced, so the difference in outcomes needs no further analysis of any kind
options.misconception: concludes a valid estimate from a balance table alone

questions.explanation: The largest gap in the table is three percentage points, and gaps of that size across three characteristics are exactly what a fair draw at this sample size produces, so the table is consistent with arms that differ only by chance. It cannot be stronger than that, because a fair draw can and does produce gaps, and a second trial would produce a different table; what randomisation supplies is the absence of a systematic direction, not a guarantee about this realisation. The useful habits are to look at the balance before believing an adjusted estimate and to remember which characteristics were never recorded, since an unrecorded one is invisible in a table like this.
questions.hint: Ask how large a gap this sample size would produce by chance alone.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Randomising an offer rather than a treatment
questions.learningObjective: explain what randomising an offer identifies and what it assumes
questions.stem: A trial cannot force anyone to take a drug, so it randomises an invitation and a reminder call instead. What does randomising the offer buy, and what must hold for the estimate to be about the drug?

options.text: Random assignment of the offer, provided the offer changes outcomes only by changing whether the drug is taken
Random assignment of the drug itself, so the estimate rests on nothing more than a fair coin
options.misconception: believes an offer randomises the treatment itself

options.text: A larger effective sample, since the units who decline the offer form a second usable control group
options.misconception: treats non-compliance as a bonus rather than a problem

options.text: Nothing, because a unit who declines the offer is indistinguishable from a unit never invited
options.misconception: denies that declining units remain a useful comparison

questions.explanation: The offer is the thing the trial can assign, and it shifts the outcome only by pushing some units into taking the drug, so a difference in outcomes between the offered and unoffered groups is a scaled version of the drug's effect rather than the drug's effect itself. The scaling is the share who take up, and dividing by it is legitimate only if the offer has no effect of its own, which is the exclusion condition and the assumption most worth arguing about. Non-compliance is not a bonus here: it is precisely what makes the estimate a scaled one, and it is why such trials are read as effects on those who take up rather than on everyone invited.
questions.hint: Ask what the invitation is a proxy for, and what would have to be false for the scaling to mislead.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The effect of the invitation itself
questions.learningObjective: compute an intention-to-treat effect from take-up rates
questions.stem: Two hundred units are invited to a drug programme; 60 take it up and average 15.0 on the outcome, and the other 140 do not take it and average 11.0. Taking the stated assumption that non-takers would not have benefited, what is the effect of the invitation?
questions.explanation: Three tenths of the invited units took the drug and each of them gained 4.0, so the effect of the invitation is 0.3 times 4.0, which is 1.2; the check from the totals gives (60 times 15.0 plus 140 times 11.0) over 200, which is 12.2, minus the 11.0 the non-takers would have had anyway, again 1.2. The 12.2 is the mean of everyone invited and is the mistake that comes from forgetting to subtract what the non-takers would have scored unaided, which turns a treatment effect into an outcome. This is the quantity a programme is actually buying, since it is what offering the drug achieves regardless of who declines it.
questions.hint: Weight the takers' gain by the share of units who took it up.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The effect among those who took it up
questions.learningObjective: recover an effect on takers from an effect of the offer
questions.stem: In the same trial, 60 of 200 invited units take the drug, and takers average 15.0 on the outcome while non-takers average 11.0. What is the estimated effect on units who took the drug because they took it?
questions.explanation: The invitation's effect of 1.2 is the drug's effect multiplied by the share who took it up, so dividing 1.2 by 0.3 gives 4.0, and the direct calculation confirms it since 15.0 minus 11.0 is also 4.0. The 1.2 is the effect of offering, which is the number for a programme deciding whether to send invitations, and 0.3 is the compliance rate, which is what converts one into the other. The estimate is only as good as the assumption that non-takers would have been unaffected, and where that assumption is doubtful the two numbers can be far apart, which is the reason to report both rather than the flattering one.
questions.hint: Divide the effect of the invitation by the share who took the drug up.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A common cause of exposure and outcome
questions.learningObjective: classify a variable as a confounder and state what follows
questions.stem: Smoking is more common among patients who recover slowly than among those who recover quickly, and the smoking habit was settled years before either recovery. What kind of variable is smoking, and what follows for a comparison?

options.text: A common cause of the treatment and the outcome, so two groups differing in it differ in more than the treatment
A consequence of the treatment, so comparing groups that differ in it removes part of the effect
options.misconception: labels a common cause as a consequence of the treatment

options.text: A consequence of both the treatment and the outcome, so comparing on it opens a path between them
options.misconception: labels a common cause as a common effect

options.text: Unrelated to the outcome, so it can be left out once the treatment has been measured carefully
options.misconception: declares a strong risk factor irrelevant because it is not the treatment

questions.explanation: A confounder is a variable with an arrow into the treatment and an arrow into the outcome, so a comparison of groups that differ in it is comparing two different kinds of people rather than two treatments, and the gap between them includes both. Smoking is settled before the outcome appears, which is what makes it usable in an adjustment rather than merely correlated. The classification is a claim about causal structure and it is not always visible in the data, which is why a diagram is drawn before the adjustment is chosen, and why two variables can be strongly associated yet belong in opposite roles.
questions.hint: Ask which arrows point into the variable, and whether the timing allows it to be adjusted for.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A variable caused by both treatment and outcome
questions.learningObjective: explain the bias created by conditioning on a common effect
questions.stem: A unit is referred to a specialist when its symptoms are severe and also when its treatment is going well, and referral is recorded for both. What does restricting attention to referred units do to a comparison of treatment and outcome?

options.text: It conditions on a common effect, opening a route between the two and manufacturing an association that was not there
It removes a common cause, so the comparison becomes less confounded than the unrestricted one
options.misconception: treats conditioning as though it always removed bias

options.text: It changes nothing, because referral happens after the outcome has already been recorded
options.misconception: believes outcome timing prevents a path from opening

options.text: It conditions on a characteristic fixed before assignment, which is the safe case to restrict to
options.misconception: confuses a post-outcome variable with a pre-treatment one

questions.explanation: Referral has two arrows coming into it, one from the treatment and one from the outcome, so restricting to referred units selects on something both were involved in producing, and that restriction is what makes the treatment and the outcome look related among the selected. The association is created by the selection rather than found in the world, and it can point either way depending on how the two arrows are signed, so it is not even predictable in advance. The general rule is that a common effect is the one variable that must not be conditioned on, and the reason a diagram is worth drawing is that a data column gives no clue which of the three roles a variable plays.
questions.hint: Draw the two arrows into the variable and ask what selecting on it does to the two other nodes.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which adjustment supports which claim
questions.learningObjective: pair a covariate with the estimand its adjustment supports
questions.stem: Two covariates are available: age, settled before assignment, and specialist referral, which follows both the treatment and the outcome. Which pairing of adjustment with claim survives scrutiny?

options.text: Adjust for age to estimate the effect of the treatment on the outcome, since age is settled first and causes both
Adjust for referral to estimate the treatment's effect, since referral is the variable nearest the outcome in time
options.misconception: believes proximity to the outcome makes a variable the right adjustment

options.text: Adjust for both and report a single effect, since more adjustment always removes more bias
options.misconception: assumes adding covariates to an adjustment can only help

options.text: Adjust for neither, since conditioning on any recorded variable is guaranteed to change the estimate
options.misconception: believes any conditioning is itself a source of bias

questions.explanation: Age sits upstream of both the treatment and the outcome, so holding it fixed removes a route by which the two could be connected without the treatment, and the estimate that survives is one for the effect within a given age. Referral sits downstream of both, so holding it fixed introduces a route that the treatment never needed, and the resulting comparison is of a selected subgroup rather than of the population. The two covariates can look equally informative in a table of correlations and belong in opposite roles, which is the whole reason the causal structure is written down before any covariate is added to a model.
questions.hint: Ask where each covariate sits relative to the treatment and the outcome in time.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Restricting to referred units
questions.learningObjective: compute the bias introduced by conditioning on a common effect
questions.stem: Among all treated units the mean outcome is 20.0 and among all control units it is 15.0. Restricting to referred units, the treated mean is 18.0 and the control mean 16.0. By how much does the restricted comparison understate the unadjusted difference?
questions.explanation: The unadjusted difference is 20.0 minus 15.0, which is 5.0, and the restricted difference is 18.0 minus 16.0, which is 2.0, so the restriction has removed 3.0 of the gap. Nothing about the treatment changed between the two comparisons; what changed is which units are in them, and the selected subgroup is one in which the treatment looks less effective because both good and bad outcomes became more likely to end up in it. This is the arithmetic signature of conditioning on a common effect, and it is the reason a restriction that looks like a sensible fairness move can quietly move the estimate in a direction nobody was looking for.
questions.hint: Compute both differences and subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Comparing users who completed a step
questions.learningObjective: identify a post-treatment variable used as a confounder
questions.stem: An analysis compares users who completed an onboarding step with users who did not, and finds a large effect on later activity. The step sits after the product change being studied. What is the flaw in reading that as the effect of the change?

options.text: The step is a consequence of the change, so the two groups were selected on how the change affected them
The step is measured after the change, so its timing by itself makes the comparison invalid
options.misconception: believes any post-change measurement disqualifies a comparison

options.text: The step is a pre-change characteristic of the user, so conditioning on it cannot bias the estimate
options.misconception: misclassifies a post-change behaviour as a pre-change trait

options.text: The step cannot be a consequence of the change, because users choose for themselves whether to finish it
options.misconception: believes user choice rules out a causal arrow from the change

questions.explanation: A change that makes the interface easier will also make more users finish the step, so the completing group is partly composed of the users the change helped, and the comparison then attributes the effect twice, once through the selection and once through the outcome. The tell is that the step is downstream of the treatment, which is exactly the position a mediator occupies, and a mediator is a legitimate object of study only when the question is about the path rather than the total effect. Comparing completers with non-completers is a good way to learn who responds, and a bad way to estimate what the change did.
questions.hint: Ask which users end up in the completing group because of the change itself.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a decision under uncertainty maximises
questions.learningObjective: explain what a decision under uncertainty maximises
questions.stem: Explain what a decision under uncertainty is supposed to maximise, and give the sentence that gets it wrong.

answer.exemplar: The quantity being maximised is the expected value of the payoff, which is the probability-weighted average across the states that can occur, not the average of the payoffs and not the best payoff that might happen. A decision rule that says a project with a small chance of a large gain is preferable to a certain moderate gain is right for that reason, and the calculation that supports it weighs the two outcomes rather than splitting the difference between them. The sentence that gets it wrong is the one that argues a launch is worth making because the good outcome is bigger than the bad one, since that compares the outcomes themselves and quietly leaves the probabilities out; if the good outcome occurs one time in fifty, its size is not the point. There is a second wrong sentence worth naming, the one that says uncertainty is a reason to wait, which confuses the absence of information with a decision to acquire it, since waiting has a cost and an information value that have to be weighed against each other explicitly.

questions.explanation: The expected value is a weighted average where the weights are the chances of each state occurring, and the two things that go wrong most often are substituting equal weights or dropping the weights altogether, which respectively answers a different question and answers none. The trap is that the unweighted average of outcomes is easy to compute and looks like prudence, and a sure moderate gain beats an unlikely large one exactly when the likelihood is low, which is the opposite of what that average suggests. Naming the states and their probabilities before computing anything is the practical defence, since a probability that was never written down is a probability that was never thought about.
questions.hint: Ask what the weights in the average are, and whether the sentence supplies any.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Expected value of launching
questions.learningObjective: compute an expected value from stated probabilities
questions.stem: A launch pays 100 units of profit if it succeeds and loses 40 units if it fails. An analyst puts the chance of success at 0.30. What is the expected value of launching?
questions.explanation: The expected value is 0.30 times 100 plus 0.70 times minus 40, which is 30 minus 28, or 2. The 30 that comes from averaging the two outcomes without weights describes a world where success and failure are equally likely, and it is the number that makes this launch look attractive; the 28 is the magnitude of the loss branch, and quoting it ignores the gain. The result being two rather than thirty is the whole lesson of the item: a large payoff does not make a project good, and the threshold any real project faces is compared against this figure, not against the best case. A sensible companion calculation is the expected value if success were 0.50, which is 30, since that shows how quickly the decision turns on the probability.
questions.hint: Weight each outcome by its probability, then add the two products.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two forecasts and a threshold
questions.learningObjective: recompute a decision when the forecast changes
questions.stem: One forecast puts the chance of success at 0.30 with a payoff of 100 on success and a loss of 40 on failure; a second puts it at 0.50 with the same payoffs. Launching costs 15 in effort either way. Which pairing of forecast and decision is defensible?

options.text: Under the second forecast the launch clears its 15 in effort and is worth making; under the first it does not and is not
The first forecast supports launching, because a chance of 0.30 for 100 outweighs a chance of 0.70 for 40
options.misconception: compares the two outcomes and leaves the probabilities out of it

options.text: Both forecasts support launching, because the average of the two payoffs is comfortably positive
options.misconception: uses the unweighted average of the outcomes as the expected value

options.text: Neither forecast supports launching, because a loss of 40 makes the expected value negative in every case
options.misconception: treats the existence of a loss branch as making every expectation negative

questions.explanation: Under the first forecast the expected value is 0.30 times 100 plus 0.70 times minus 40, which is 2, and 2 does not cover 15, so the launch loses money on average; under the second it is 0.50 times 100 plus 0.50 times minus 40, which is 30, and 30 clears 15. The two forecasts therefore imply opposite decisions, which is the honest state of affairs when the disagreement is a disagreement about probability rather than about arithmetic, and the response is to go and find out which forecast is better founded rather than to average them. Averaging the forecasts, or averaging the outcomes, produces a number that corresponds to no forecast anyone holds and so supports no decision at all.
questions.hint: Compute the expected value under each forecast, then subtract the 15 in effort from each.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: From a claim to a defensible estimate
questions.learningObjective: order the stages that turn an observational claim into an estimate
questions.stem: A team has an observational comparison and a causal claim it wants to defend. Put these four stages in the order that gets from the claim to a number somebody else could check.

options.text: State the causal quantity wanted and the population it should apply to, before looking at any comparison
Draw the assumed causal structure, marking causes, consequences and any variable caused by both
Choose how the quantity will be identified, such as random assignment or a comparison the data supplies
Estimate the quantity and report beside the number the assumption the estimate rests on

questions.explanation: The estimand comes first because a number without a stated population and quantity is not an answer to anything, and the diagram comes before the method because the role of each variable, settled in advance, is what decides what may be adjusted for. Identification is then a claim about which comparison stands in for the missing half, and only once that claim is written down does it make sense to compute, with the assumption reported beside the result so a reader can disagree with the claim rather than with the arithmetic. The order that starts with the estimate and works backwards is the common failure, since a number computed before its target is fixed tends to answer whichever question the data made easy.
questions.hint: Ask which stage a reader would need in order to disagree with the others.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The quantity a difference in differences estimates
questions.learningObjective: state what a difference in differences compares
questions.stem: A region introduces a programme in 2021 and a similar region does not, and outcomes are recorded for both in 2019 and in 2023. What quantity does a difference in differences estimate?

options.text: The treated region's change between the two years minus the comparison region's change over the same span
The treated region's 2023 outcome minus the comparison region's 2023 outcome in that same year
options.misconception: reads a cross-section of one year as the design's estimate

options.text: The treated region's 2023 outcome minus its own 2019 outcome, which is the programme's effect
options.misconception: uses before-and-after within one region as the estimate

options.text: The two regions' average outcomes across both years, which nets out their fixed difference
options.misconception: substitutes a two-year average for a change in a difference

questions.explanation: The design takes the difference between the regions after the programme and subtracts the difference between them before, which in this case is a change in a gap rather than a gap or a change. The two wrong subtractions are the two that the design exists to avoid: comparing one year across regions leaves any permanent difference between them in the answer, and comparing one region across years leaves everything else that moved in that region in the answer. What the untreated region supplies is not a measurement of the counterfactual but a stand-in for the path the treated region would have followed, and how good that stand-in is the assumption the whole design rests on.
questions.hint: Ask how many differences the calculation takes and over which years each is measured.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The assumption a difference in differences cannot observe
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption that lets a comparison region stand in for a counterfactual
questions.stem: A difference in differences is read as the programme's effect. What has to be true of the two regions for the untreated region's change to stand in for the treated region's missing path?

options.text: That without the programme both regions would have moved by the same amount, which the design never observes
That the two regions had identical outcomes in 2019, which is what makes their changes comparable
options.misconception: equates a level match with a parallel change

options.text: That the programme began at the same time in both regions, which the design requires
options.misconception: invents a symmetry requirement the design does not impose

options.text: That neither region's population changed between the years, which is what rules out composition shifts
options.misconception: substitutes a composition requirement for the trend assumption

questions.explanation: The untreated region is being asked to play the part of the treated region in the years after the programme, and the only version of that role that makes the subtraction meaningful is one where the two would have moved together, so a difference in the movement is what the programme did. The assumption is untestable in the treated region after the fact, which is why pre-programme years are collected and plotted, and why a design with several pre-periods is preferred to one with a single. Two regions can be at very different levels in 2019 and still satisfy the assumption, which is why the level match is not the requirement.
questions.hint: Ask what the untreated region would have had to do for its change to be informative.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The difference in differences estimate
questions.learningObjective: compute a difference in differences from four figures
questions.stem: One region's outcome is 60 in 2019 and 72 in 2023. A comparison region's outcome is 50 in 2019 and 53 in 2023. What does a difference in differences give as the estimate?
questions.explanation: The treated region changed by 12 and the comparison region by 3, so the estimate is 12 minus 3, which is 9, and rearranging to (72 - 53) minus (60 - 50) gives 19 minus 10 and the same 9. The 12 is the before-and-after change in the treated region, which is the figure that appears when the design's subtraction is forgotten, and it is larger than the estimate precisely because the comparison region's own rise of 3 is being attributed to the programme. The 3 on its own is the comparison region's change, and 19 is the two regions' gap after the programme, which is a cross-section and not a causal estimate.
questions.hint: Take each region's change and subtract the comparison region's change from the treated region's.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A pre-programme table inside the report
questions.learningObjective: interpret evidence that a design's own assumption fails
questions.stem: A report estimates a programme's effect at 9 points by difference in differences and calls it causal. Its own table shows the treated region at 60 in 2019 and 61 in 2020, and the comparison region at 50 in both years. What does that table do to the claim?

options.text: It shows the two regions already moving apart before the programme, which is the design's own assumption failing
It shows the two regions moving together beforehand, which is direct support for the assumption
options.misconception: reads a widening pre-trend as evidence of parallel trends

options.text: It shows the programme began earlier than stated, so the estimate covers a different period
options.misconception: reinterprets a pre-trend as a dating error

options.text: It shows the comparison region is an unsuitable unit, so a better one should be chosen instead
options.misconception: prescribes a new comparison without addressing the failure

questions.explanation: The treated region rose by one point in the year before the programme while the comparison region did not move, so the two were on diverging paths before the programme existed, and the untreated region's change is therefore an implausible stand-in for the path the treated region was already leaving. The 9-point estimate is then the sum of the programme and a gap that opened in advance, and reporting it as the programme's effect attributes to the programme a difference that predates it. This is the reason to collect several pre-periods and plot them, and the reason a report that publishes its own pre-trend table has made the problem visible rather than hidden.

questions.topic: The jump at a threshold
questions.learningObjective: compute an effect from the two sides of a threshold
questions.stem: Support is granted automatically at a score of 70. Among 60 units just above the threshold the mean outcome is 18.4, and among 58 units just below it the mean is 12.0. What is the estimated effect of crossing the threshold?

The 1.53 is the ratio of the two means, which answers a different question, and both means on their own describe one side of the rule rather than the effect of crossing it. The argument for using this design at all is that the two sides are made up of units with almost identical scores, so the comparison is between near-neighbours rather than between two kinds of unit, and everything therefore rests on the assumption that the outcome would have carried on smoothly across the threshold without the rule.

The treatment had no effect, since a gap in the density of scores is a gap in the outcome
options.misconception: confuses the density of the running variable with the outcome

options.misconception: presumes a density gap is evidence of an administrative error

questions.topic: The estimate produced by a synthetic control
questions.learningObjective: state what a synthetic control estimates and why the pre-period gap matters
questions.stem: One region is treated and no comparable unit exists, so a weighted blend of untreated regions is built to reproduce its history. What is the estimate, and what makes it persuasive?

options.text: The post-period gap between the region and the blend, after subtracting the gap the blend already had beforehand
The region's post-period level, since the blend exists only to give that level a scale to read on
options.misconception: reports the treated level as the estimate

options.text: The blend's post-period average, which is the untreated path the region was heading along
options.misconception: reports the counterfactual itself as the estimate

options.text: The region's post-period level minus its own pre-period level, which the blend was not needed for
options.misconception: uses before-and-after within the treated region alone

questions.explanation: A blend that already sits a little above the region before the intervention would make the post-period gap look larger than the intervention's doing, so the pre-period gap is subtracted out and the estimate is the change in the gap. Subtracting nothing leaves the fit error inside the answer, and quoting the blend's own level throws away the whole construction by reporting the counterfactual rather than the difference from it. What makes the result persuasive is not the construction but the fit: a blend that reproduces several pre-intervention years closely, and does so with weights that are a genuine combination of donors rather than one donor in disguise, is a comparison worth reading.
questions.hint: Ask what the gap looked like before the intervention, and whether that has come out of the answer.

questions.topic: A synthetic control net of its own fit
questions.learningObjective: compute a synthetic control estimate net of the pre-period gap
questions.stem: A synthetic control's blend exceeds a treated region's outcome by 1.0, 1.3 and 1.3 in the three years before the intervention, and by 7.0 and 8.2 in the two years after it. What is the estimated effect of the intervention?
questions.explanation: The pre-intervention excess averages (1.0 + 1.3 + 1.3) over 3, which is 1.2, and the post-intervention excess averages (7.0 + 8.2) over 2, which is 7.6, so the effect is 7.6 minus 1.2, or 6.4. The 7.6 is the post-period gap taken on its own, which leaves the blend's original 1.2 advantage inside the estimate, and the 8.8 is what results from adding the pre-period gap instead of removing it. A gap of 1.2 before an intervention is a small fit error, and it is worth subtracting because the alternative reading treats a mismatch the researcher chose to accept as though the programme had created it.
questions.hint: Average each period's excess and subtract the earlier average from the later one.

questions.topic: Running the same procedure on the untreated regions
questions.learningObjective: interpret a placebo test of a synthetic control
questions.stem: A synthetic control is built for a treated region, and the same procedure is then run for every untreated region in the donor pool, each with its own placebo intervention date. What does the pattern of placebo results establish?

options.text: Whether the treated region's post-period gap stands out from what the same procedure produces for units with no intervention
That the treated region's gap is the largest, which by itself proves the intervention worked
options.misconception: treats a maximum across placebos as proof of an effect

options.text: That the blend is well specified, since every region can be matched to some weighted blend of the others
options.misconception: assumes matching is informative when it is done by construction

options.text: That the effect is zero for the untreated regions, since their own pre-period gaps were removed
options.misconception: assumes the placebo gaps vanish once the pre-period is removed

A large gap in a placebo region is evidence that the construction produces gaps without any intervention, which is exactly what makes the treated region's gap interpretable. The largest gap in the pool is not proof, because with twenty or thirty placebos the largest one is expected to be large by chance, and the count of placebos that reach the treated region's gap is the figure to report.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A propensity score and what it must satisfy
questions.learningObjective: state the overlap requirement behind weighting on a propensity score
questions.stem: A propensity score is the probability that a unit takes the treatment given its measured characteristics. What has to hold before units can be compared by weighting or matching on that score?

options.text: The scores must overlap, so that every treated unit has untreated units whose characteristics look like its own
The scores must average the same value in both groups, which is what balance on the score requires
options.misconception: equates a shared average with full overlap

options.text: The scores must sit near one half, since a score far from a half means weak characteristics
options.misconception: reads the score's position as a measure of the covariates

options.text: The scores must be linear in the characteristics, since a nonlinear score cannot be compared across units
options.misconception: imposes a functional form on a probability

questions.explanation: Weighting and matching both work by finding comparison units that resemble the treated unit, and they can only do that where the two score distributions share a range, so a treated unit at 0.92 with no untreated unit above 0.6 has no comparison available at any weight. Two units with the same score are balanced on the measured characteristics by construction, which is the score's usefulness, and overlap is the condition that makes such units exist. A common average across the groups is a much weaker statement than overlap, since the two distributions can share a mean and still barely touch, and the units in the tail are exactly the ones a shared mean conceals.
questions.hint: Ask whether a comparison unit exists for every treated unit, not whether the averages agree.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a doubly robust estimator is doubly robust
questions.learningObjective: explain the source of a doubly robust estimator's robustness
questions.stem: A study fits both a model of who takes the treatment and a model of the outcome, and combines them so that only one of the two has to be right. Which pairing of property and reason survives scrutiny?

options.text: The estimate stays unbiased if either model is right, because the two sets of errors cannot both point the same way
The estimate has a smaller standard error, since two models average away each other's noise
options.misconception: confuses robustness with precision

options.text: The estimate uses more of the data, since both models are fitted on the full sample rather than a subset
options.misconception: attributes the property to sample size rather than structure

options.text: The estimate is unbiased regardless, since checking two models removes the need for either of them
options.misconception: reads conditional robustness as unconditional validity

questions.explanation: There are two ways the estimate can go wrong and the construction is arranged so that each model is what neutralises the other one's failure, so a study that gets the outcome model wrong is rescued by a correct treatment model and vice versa, and a study that gets both wrong is not rescued. The sentence to distrust is the one that says checking two models removes the need for either, since what the pair removes is the need for both to be right, which is a weaker and more useful thing. In practice this makes a doubly robust estimate a good default when both models are easy to fit, and it is also why reporting which of the two was checked is worth the extra work.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when exactly one of the two models is wrong, and who corrects for it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a matching procedure leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: identify the imbalance a matching procedure can leave
questions.stem: Treated units are matched to untreated units on a propensity score, and the matched groups now have the same average score. What is still unproven, and what should be checked next?

options.text: Balance on the individual characteristics, since units can share a score while differing on the parts that produced it
The correctness of the score itself, since equal averages prove the model was right in every respect
options.misconception: treats a shared average as proof of a correctly specified model

options.text: That the matching was random, since a deterministic rule on the score cannot be a random assignment
options.misconception: requires random assignment from a method that never promised it

options.text: That the outcome model is linear, since matching cannot be combined with any outcome model at all
options.misconception: believes matching rules out modelling the outcome

questions.explanation: A propensity score compresses several characteristics into one number, so two units with identical scores can be alike on average across the characteristics and different on each, and a matching rule that only sees the score will happily pair such units. The diagnostic is to return to the characteristics themselves and measure how far apart the matched groups now are, standardised so that the units are comparable, and to match on the score while also checking that list. That is also where the honest reporting requirement sits, because a matching procedure whose balance is never shown has not demonstrated the property it was chosen for.
questions.hint: Ask what a single score can hide, and which table would reveal it.

questions.topic: Treated units with no comparison available
questions.learningObjective: count the units that an overlap requirement excludes
questions.stem: Ten treated units have propensity scores of 0.05, 0.12, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70, 0.82 and 0.91, and the highest score among the untreated units is 0.75. How many treated units have no untreated unit with a score at least as high?
questions.explanation: A treated unit can only borrow a comparison from an untreated unit whose score is at least as high, and the two treated units at 0.82 and 0.91 sit above the untreated maximum of 0.75, so 2 of the 10 have no available comparison. The other numbers are the traps: reporting 1 comes from comparing against the highest untreated score and forgetting that two units sit above it, and 10 comes from concluding that a score of 0.05 is unmatched because it is at the bottom rather than at the top. The practical consequence is a report that quietly drops a fifth of the treated group, which is a different estimand from the one originally stated and has to be said out loud.
questions.hint: Count the treated scores that exceed the highest untreated score.

questions.learningObjective: read an overlap plot and identify missing coverage

Nothing, since the two ranges are close and close ranges mean the groups are comparable everywhere
options.misconception: reads similar widths as complete coverage

options.text: The plot proves the characteristics are balanced, since a propensity score summarises all of them
options.misconception: treats a score as a balance check in its own right

options.text: The groups are not comparable because the untreated range is narrower, which is what overlap requires
options.misconception: defines overlap as equal width rather than shared support

That is a real finding and not a failure, provided it is reported, because the units in the tail are often exactly the ones with the strongest indication and excluding them can move the estimate in a chosen direction. The habit to avoid is treating a picture of two histograms as a balance check, which is a separate measurement made on the characteristics themselves.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Balance after matching in one number
questions.learningObjective: compute a standardised mean difference
questions.stem: After matching, the treated units have a mean age of 39.0 and the untreated units 38.0, with a pooled standard deviation of 6.0. Before matching the same measure was 1.0. What is the standardised mean difference after matching?
questions.explanation: The standardised mean difference is the gap divided by a standard deviation expressed in the same units, so 39.0 minus 38.0 is 1.0 and 1.0 over 6.0 is 0.167; the check from the raw totals gives the same figure, since 1560 over 40 and 1520 over 40 are the two means and the pooled sum of squared deviations of 2844 over 79 degrees of freedom is a standard deviation of exactly 6. The 1.0 before matching is the same measure on a worse pairing, and the fall from 1.0 to 0.167 is the evidence that matching did something. The remaining 0.167 is still a fifth of the pre-matching gap, which is why a threshold such as a tenth is applied and why a result reported without the balance figures leaves the reader unable to judge it.
questions.hint: Take the difference between the two means and divide it by the pooled standard deviation.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A monthly series around a change
questions.learningObjective: interpret an interrupted time series and its trend assumption
questions.stem: A monthly outcome runs 40, 42, 41, 44, 43 before a change in June and 46, 47, 52, 55, 57 after it. An interrupted time series reports a level change of 3 and a trend change of 1.5 a month. What does the reported trend change rest on?

options.text: The assumption that the pre-change trend would have continued unchanged, which five months of data cannot establish
The assumption that the post-change trend is constant, which the rising monthly values contradict
options.misconception: assumes a constant post-change trend the values themselves violate

options.text: A comparison of the post-change level with the pre-change level, which needs no assumption about trend
options.misconception: claims the trend estimate is free of a trend assumption

options.text: The measured change in level at June, which is observed directly and involves no extrapolation
options.misconception: confuses the level change with the trend change

Five pre-change months rising from 40 to 43 give a slope, but no slope estimated from that little data can be defended against a secular change in the underlying process, which is the threat that makes these series so fragile. A longer pre-period, a control series, and a check for other events in the period are what make the reported trend change more than an extrapolation.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Stating a design's assumption honestly
questions.learningObjective: explain what parallel trends does and does not assert
questions.stem: Explain what parallel trends does and does not assert in a difference in differences, and give the sentence that overstates it.

answer.exemplar: Parallel trends says that the two groups would have moved by the same amount between the two measurement points had the programme not arrived, which is a claim about changes and not about levels, so two groups can sit at 60 and 50 before the programme and still satisfy it. It does not say the two groups are similar, and it does not say the assumption has been checked, because nothing in the data after the programme can test it; the only evidence available is the record of the two groups before the programme, and that record can support or undermine the assumption without settling it. The sentence that overstates it says the comparison region is a genuine control group, as though naming something a control made it one, when the region is a control only to the extent that its untreated path happens to parallel the treated region's, which is the assumption doing all of the work. A second overstatement is saying the assumption was verified because the pre-programme lines look close, when what a plot of pre-programme years can do is raise or lower confidence in an assumption about a period nobody observed.

questions.explanation: The assumption concerns a counterfactual path that is never observed, so every check of it is indirect, which is why honest statements of it are about evidence and confidence rather than about verification. The distinction between changes and levels is the part most often lost, since a design can be valid with two very differently sized regions, and a design can be invalid with two that started almost identical. The overstating sentence is the one that converts a name into a guarantee, and the second is the one that turns suggestive pre-trend evidence into proof.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about levels or about changes, and what evidence could possibly bear on it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a sensitivity analysis varies
questions.learningObjective: explain the parameter a sensitivity analysis varies and what it reveals
questions.stem: Explain what a sensitivity analysis varies in a causal estimate, and give the sentence that misdescribes it.

answer.exemplar: A sensitivity analysis varies the one quantity the estimate depends on that the data cannot pin down, most often the strength of an unmeasured confounder expressed as how much its two groups would have to differ for the estimate to change sign, and then reports the value at which the conclusion flips. That is the point: the analysis converts an unanswerable question about the world into a number a reader can argue about, and a study that reports how fragile its conclusion is has given the reader more than one that reports a bare estimate with no acknowledged assumption. The sentence that misdescribes it says the analysis checks that the result is robust, which inverts the purpose, since a sensitivity analysis is run precisely because robustness is unknown and its output is often a finding that the result is fragile. A second misdescription treats the varied parameter as a nuisance to be tuned until the answer holds, which turns a probe of the evidence into a search for a comfortable setting and is why the varied value is reported rather than chosen.

questions.explanation: The varied parameter is a stand-in for what is not in the data, and the reportable output is the value at which the conclusion would change, which is a fact about how much evidence the study has rather than a restatement of the estimate. The misdescribing sentence is the one about checking robustness, because it promises reassurance the analysis cannot deliver and because a study that needs to be shown to be robust has already conceded that it might not be. Reporting the flipping value is what lets a reader decide whether the fragility matters for the decision at hand.
questions.hint: Ask what the analysis varies, and what the value at which the answer flips tells the reader.

questions.topic: A series with a change in the middle
questions.learningObjective: state what an interrupted time series identifies and what threatens it
questions.stem: A monthly outcome is recorded for two years and a change is introduced partway through, and the analysis fits a level and a trend before and after. What does the design identify, and what is the threat to it?

options.text: A level change and a trend change, threatened by any other process moving the series over the same period
A level change only, threatened by a change in the number of observations before and after the change
options.misconception: misidentifies what the two slopes give

options.text: A trend change only, threatened by a level shift that the specification is unable to absorb
options.misconception: leaves out the level change the design can also estimate

options.text: The effect of the change, threatened only by the small number of observations after it
options.misconception: insists the only threat is the sample size

questions.explanation: Fitting a straight line before and after the change gives two differences rather than one, a level shift and a change in slope, and the second is the fragile one because the counterfactual slope has to be projected from the pre-period rather than measured. That projection is the threat: a policy introduced alongside a budget cycle, a price change, or a competitor's launch will be credited with whatever the underlying process was already doing, and no amount of care in the fit distinguishes them. Long pre-periods, a control series, and a record of other events in the window are what make the result something other than a description of a curve that bent.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two estimated quantities depends on projecting the pre-period forward.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What an instrumental variable has to satisfy
questions.learningObjective: state the two conditions an instrumental variable must satisfy
questions.stem: A lottery decides which patients are offered a second appointment, and patients cannot refuse the offer. What are the two conditions the lottery has to satisfy for the ratio of the two effects to be read as the effect of attending?

options.text: It must change attendance, and it must change nothing else about the outcome that could affect it
It must change attendance, and every patient must in fact attend the appointment they are offered
options.misconception: requires full compliance rather than a first condition

options.text: It must be assigned independently of health, and patients offered an appointment must attend at the same rate
options.misconception: adds a compliance requirement the ratio does not need

options.text: It must be unpredictable, and it must be offered to every patient in the study population
options.misconception: confuses randomisation with complete coverage

questions.explanation: The first condition is that the lottery moves treatment, which is checked by asking whether being offered an appointment actually changes attendance, and the second is that it moves nothing else that could affect the outcome, which is a claim about the offer rather than about the appointment. The second is the assumption nobody can verify, since the only way to check it would be to know what the offer does apart from the appointment, and a lottery that shortens a waiting list or reassures a patient has failed it. It is also why the ratio is read as an effect on those who attend rather than on everyone, since the lottery only rearranges attendance for people whose attendance the lottery can move.
questions.hint: Ask what the instrument must move, and what it must leave alone.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The ratio of a reduced form to a first stage
questions.learningObjective: compute a ratio estimate from a reduced form and a first stage
questions.stem: A lottery offers an appointment to some patients. In the high-lottery group 60 per cent attend and the mean outcome is 15.0, and in the low-lottery group 40 per cent attend and the mean is 13.4. What is the ratio estimate of the effect of attending?
questions.explanation: The lottery moves attendance by 0.60 minus 0.40, which is 0.20, and it moves the outcome by 15.0 minus 13.4, which is 1.60, and 1.60 over 0.20 is 8. The 1.60 on its own is the effect of the lottery, and the 0.20 on its own is the effect of the lottery on attendance, and neither is the effect of attending, which is why the ratio of the two is taken rather than either figure. The 1.25 comes from dividing 0.20 by 1.60, which inverts the ratio and is the most common slip in this calculation, and the estimate is 8 rather than the group's own gap of 1.6 because attendance is not assigned by the lottery but the appointment is.
questions.hint: Take the change in the outcome and divide it by the change in attendance.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An effect that differs across subgroups
questions.learningObjective: compute an average effect weighted by subgroup sizes
questions.stem: Four subgroups have estimated effects of 0.10, 0.20, 0.00 and 0.30, and contain 200, 300, 100 and 400 units respectively. What is the average effect over the study population?
questions.explanation: The population average weights each subgroup by how many units it holds, so (0.10 times 200) plus (0.20 times 300) plus (0.00 times 100) plus (0.30 times 400) over 1000 is 200 over 1000, which is 0.20. The 0.15 is the unweighted mean of the four figures, which answers a different question, since a study population in which the fourth subgroup is twice the size of the first is not described by the average of four numbers. The 0.30 is the largest subgroup effect, which is a claim about one group and not about the population, and 0.10 is the smallest. What the spread itself says is worth more than any of these figures, since an effect of 0.30 for one group and 0.00 for another is a stronger argument for targeting than the average is.
questions.hint: Weight each subgroup's effect by its number of units, then divide by the total.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The cost of a screening threshold
questions.learningObjective: compute the expected cost of the errors a threshold makes
questions.stem: A screening rule flags 40 of the 60 true cases and 30 of the 940 units with no case. A missed case costs 200 and a false alarm costs 10. What is the total cost of the rule's two kinds of error?
questions.explanation: Missing 20 of the 60 true cases costs 20 times 200, which is 4000, and flagging 30 units with no case costs 30 times 10, which is 300, so the total is 4300. The 70 counts the flags rather than the errors, and 300 would result from treating the false alarms as though there were 30 times as many of them. What makes the arithmetic worth doing is the asymmetry it exposes: at these costs one missed case is worth twenty false alarms, so a rule that catches fewer cases but raises the flag rate is cheap, and the threshold should move accordingly. A rule is therefore never evaluated on its accuracy alone, since a highly accurate rule can be the most expensive one available.
questions.hint: Count the missed cases and the false alarms, then weight each by its own cost.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What perfect information would be worth
questions.learningObjective: compute the value of perfect information
questions.stem: Demand will be strong with probability 0.6, giving a return of 100, or weak with probability 0.4, giving 20. What is the expected value of perfect information about demand, in the same units?
questions.explanation: Without information the expected value is 0.6 times 100 plus 0.4 times 20, which is 68, and with perfect information the decision follows the state and gives 100 in either, so the difference is 32; the same figure is the probability of the state you would not have chosen, 0.4, times the gap between the two returns, 80. The 68 is the expected value without the information rather than the value of getting it, and 100 is the return that perfect information delivers rather than what the information is worth. The useful comparison is with what a study or a pilot would cost, since a 32 ceiling means no purchase of information can be worth more than that however it is obtained.
questions.hint: Compare the best expected return without information against the return perfect information would secure.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The alternative a choice displaces
questions.learningObjective: compute a net value net of the forgone alternative
questions.stem: Option A pays 120 for a cost of 30, and the best use of the same 30 is an option that pays 80 for a cost of 35. What is the net value of choosing A rather than its alternative?
questions.explanation: A returns 90 net and the alternative returns 45 net, and A is therefore worth 45 more than what it displaces, which is the figure a decision needs when only one can be chosen. The 90 is A's net return and is the number a comparison that ignores the alternative would report, and 75 is what A pays before its own cost is deducted, which is a gross figure and answers nothing about a choice. The 45 also happens to be the alternative's own net return, since A pays 40 more gross for 5 less cost, and the coincidence is arithmetic rather than a rule, so the general form is the difference of the two net returns.
questions.hint: Take each option's return net of its own cost, then subtract the better from the worse and reverse it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Discounting a year of waiting
questions.learningObjective: compute the discounted value of waiting against acting now
questions.stem: Building now costs 100 and returns 130 a year later, giving 30 net today. Waiting a year costs 110 and returns 150 at the end of that year, giving 40 net, discounted at 25 per cent. How much better is waiting, in today's units?
questions.explanation: Waiting is worth 40 discounted by a factor of 1.25, which is 32 in today's units, and 32 against 30 for building now leaves 2 in favour of waiting, so the delay pays but only just. The 40 is the undiscounted figure and the 10 is the gap before discounting rather than after, and the whole calculation turns on the rate: a discount of a third would make waiting worth 30 and the two options would be exactly level, which is the point at which the choice stops being about numbers. Discounting a reversible decision is also a different exercise from discounting a permanent one, because the option to act again next year is worth something the calculation above does not include.
questions.hint: Discount the waiting option's net return, then subtract the net return of acting now.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What waiting is worth when the branch is unknown
questions.learningObjective: compute the value of the option to wait
questions.stem: Building now costs 60 and returns 80, giving 20 net for certain. Waiting a year reveals the market: with probability 0.5 the build is then worth 90 net, and with probability 0.5 it is better not to build, giving 0. What is the option to wait worth over and above building now?
questions.explanation: Waiting is worth 0.5 times 90 plus 0.5 times 0, which is 45 in expectation, and building now is worth 20 with certainty, so the option is worth 45 minus 20, which is 25. The same figure falls out of pricing it branch by branch: in the good branch the wait beats building by 70 and in the bad branch it beats it by 20, and 0.5 times 70 plus 0.5 times 20 is 25. The 45 is the expected value of waiting rather than the value of the option, and 20 is what building now is worth, so quoting either alone loses the comparison that gives the option its value, which is the freedom not to commit while the branch is still unknown.
questions.hint: Work out the expected value of waiting, subtract what building now is worth, and check branch by branch.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Proportion of flagged records that are true
questions.learningObjective: compute the precision of a score-based rule
questions.stem: There are 20,000 accounts, 400 of which are frauds. A score flags the top 5 per cent, which is 1,000 accounts, and 60 of those flagged accounts are frauds. What proportion of the flagged accounts are actually frauds?
questions.explanation: The flagged set holds 1,000 accounts of which 60 are frauds, so the proportion is 60 over 1000, which is 0.06, and the check is that the other 940 are false alarms and 940 over 1000 is 0.94. The 0.02 is the base rate across all accounts, which is the number a reader reaches for when the question is about how common fraud is rather than about how good the rule is. The 0.15 is the fraction of frauds the rule catches, which is a different and complementary quantity, and a report that quotes the base rate beside a precision of 6 per cent is making the argument that a rule at that threshold generates far more work than cases.
questions.hint: Divide the flagged accounts that are frauds by the total number of flagged accounts.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A forest of subgroup estimates
questions.learningObjective: interpret a display of subgroup estimates with intervals
questions.stem: A display shows four subgroup estimates with intervals: 0.30 from 0.15 to 0.45, 0.20 from 0.05 to 0.35, 0.12 from minus 0.10 to 0.34, and 0.08 from minus 0.15 to 0.31. What can be said about the subgroups?

options.text: The first is separated from zero, the fourth is not, and no pair of the four is clearly distinguished from the others
The four are ordered from strongest to weakest, so the effect falls as the subgroup gets smaller
options.misconception: reads a ranking of point estimates as significant differences

options.text: All four are positive, since every point estimate lies above zero and the intervals are wide
options.misconception: ignores the intervals and reads the point estimates

options.text: The effect is uniform, since the intervals for all four overlap heavily with each other
options.misconception: turns overlapping intervals into a claim of no variation

questions.explanation: An interval that excludes zero is the ordinary test for whether that subgroup shows an effect, and only the first qualifies here, while the fourth's interval spans zero comfortably and the middle two sit close to the line. The four intervals overlap each other so heavily that the display does not establish the first subgroup as different from the fourth, and a table of point estimates in a tidy descending order is exactly the arrangement that tempts a reader to claim a gradient. The honest reading is one effect of uncertain size, possibly varying by subgroup, and a decision about whether the variation is real requires a comparison across the estimates rather than a rank order of their middles.
questions.hint: Ask which intervals exclude zero, and then ask whether the intervals separate each other.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a score does to the people it scores
questions.learningObjective: interpret the incentives a deployed scoring rule creates
questions.stem: A fraud score is used to hold accounts for review. Six months after deployment, the accounts flagged are mostly held accounts, and the review queue fills with accounts that would never have been reviewed. What does the pattern show?

options.text: The rule is measuring the outcome it produces, since being held is what now makes an account look like a fraud
The rule has improved, since a queue of held accounts is what a working detector looks like
options.misconception: reads the effect of the rule as evidence it is detecting better

options.text: The queue shows the threshold is too high, since a fuller queue always means too few accounts are being flagged
options.misconception: judges a threshold from the volume of work alone

options.text: The accounts are mislabelled, since an account can only be a fraud if the review confirmed it first
options.misconception: denies that the rule's own action can define its label

questions.explanation: Once a score is used to act, the action changes the thing the score predicts, so the population of flagged accounts fills with accounts that were flagged and then held, and the model learns from that population that held accounts resemble frauds. Over successive rounds the rule is increasingly measuring its own past decisions, which is the loop that makes a deployed score look like it is improving while the underlying rate of fraud is flat. The remedies are structural rather than statistical, such as keeping a hold-out group that is never acted on, or sampling reviews regardless of the score, so that the label never becomes a consequence of the prediction.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the flagged accounts after the rule acted on them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A loop that runs through the data
questions.learningObjective: identify a feedback loop in a measured outcome
questions.stem: A lending model sets a credit limit, and the limit determines how much a borrower can take on. Years later the model's predicted default rate for that borrower is computed from the limit itself. What has happened to the inputs?

options.text: The limit the model chose became an input to the outcome the model predicts, so the two can no longer be separated
The limit is an external factor, so including it in the prediction leaves the model's accuracy unchanged
options.misconception: denies that an action can become an input

options.text: The model is self-fulfilling, so its accuracy is now guaranteed and no further validation is needed
options.misconception: turns a feedback loop into a claim of correctness

options.text: The borrower chose the limit, so the loop only exists for borrowers who accepted an offer
options.misconception: attributes the limit to the customer rather than the model

questions.explanation: The model set a quantity, the quantity shaped what the customer did, and the outcome the model scores is measured on a world in which its own past decision is already embedded, so the two are entangled and the historical data no longer describes the situation the model is being used in. That is why a model whose predictions help create its own outcomes needs a different validation strategy, since the accuracy measured on the past is partly a record of its own influence on the past. A hold-out group never exposed to the action, or a design that randomises the limit, is what breaks the loop and restores a comparison that means something.
questions.hint: Ask whether the quantity the model set is also something the model later reads.
