questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Adjusting for a variable on the path
questions.learningObjective: explain how conditioning on a mediator changes the estimand
questions.stem: An education programme raises qualifications, and qualifications raise earnings. An analysis that adjusts for qualifications reports a much smaller effect on earnings than one that does not. What has the adjusted analysis estimated?

options.text: The effect of the programme among people who already have the same qualifications, which is not the programme's total effect
The total effect of the programme, since holding qualifications fixed removes the noise rather than the effect
options.misconception: assumes an adjustment on the path removes only confounding

options.text: The effect of the programme on qualifications, which the adjusted earnings figure also reports
options.misconception: confuses the outcome being adjusted with the outcome being estimated

options.text: No effect at all, since a result that shrinks under adjustment was always confounded to begin with
options.misconception: treats a change under adjustment as proof of confounding

questions.explanation: Qualifications sit between the programme and earnings, so holding them fixed closes part of the route by which the programme works, and what remains is the effect among people who reached the same qualification level by other routes. That is a real and sometimes interesting quantity, but it is not the programme's total effect, and reporting it as the programme's effect gives away the mechanism the programme was built on. The general rule is that an adjustment is legitimate for causes fixed before the treatment and illegitimate for consequences of it, and the diagnostic is a question about arrows rather than about whether the estimate got smaller.
questions.hint: Ask whether the adjusted variable is a cause that precedes the treatment or a consequence of it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Choosing where a rule should cut
questions.learningObjective: reason about a threshold with asymmetric costs
questions.stem: A referral rule flags accounts for review. A missed case costs 200 and a false alarm costs 10, and the flag rate rises with the threshold. What is the defensible pairing of a threshold and an argument?

options.text: Set the threshold low enough to catch most cases, since a missed case outweighs twenty false alarms in cost
Set the threshold high, since accuracy improves as fewer accounts are flagged and accuracy is the right measure here
options.misconception: chooses accuracy while the costs are heavily asymmetric

options.text: Set the threshold to flag five per cent of accounts, since a fixed share is the fairest rule to apply
options.misconception: uses a quota rather than the costs to set the threshold

options.text: Set the threshold to flag no accounts, since a rule that flags nothing makes no errors of either kind
options.misconception: treats abstention as error-free

questions.explanation: The right threshold is the one that minimises total cost, and with one missed case worth twenty false alarms the calculation will always favour casting a wide net, because the extra flags are cheap next to the cases they catch. Accuracy is the wrong measure precisely because it treats the two errors as equally serious, and a rule can be highly accurate while missing most of the cases that matter. A fixed share is a fairness consideration rather than a cost calculation, and abstaining avoids the cost of review while forfeiting the benefit of catching anything, which is a real choice but not the one the numbers here support.
questions.hint: Ask which measure of performance matches the two costs, and compare the two errors directly.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The alternative a choice gives up
questions.learningObjective: explain opportunity cost as a real cost of a decision
questions.stem: Explain what opportunity cost is, why it is not the same as the cost a decision shows on its invoice, and give the sentence that hides it.

answer.exemplar: The cost of a decision is everything it gives up, and the part that never appears anywhere is the value of the best thing the resources would otherwise have produced, which is why two decisions can have identical invoices and completely different costs. The invoice records what was paid; the forgone alternative is what the same money or the same week would have earned, and it is a real amount that a decision maker will feel later, which is exactly what makes it invisible in the comparison people usually make. The sentence that hides it says the cheaper option is therefore the sensible one, since that compares two payments rather than two outcomes and quietly assumes the resources would have done nothing otherwise, which is the assumption least likely to be true. The practical consequence is that a decision whose benefit is hard to name is often the one whose forgone alternative is largest, because an unquantified benefit is easier to overlook than an unquantified cost, and the standard remedy is to name the alternative explicitly before the decision rather than after it.

questions.explanation: The distinction is between a payment and a consequence, and only the second belongs in a decision, which is why a cost-benefit comparison that stops at the invoice will systematically favour whichever option spends less and earns less. The forgone alternative is not always easy to value, and that is a genuine difficulty rather than a reason to ignore it, since the options that look obviously worse once the alternative is named are often the ones that were attractive precisely because the alternative was not named. Naming it before the decision is what keeps the comparison honest.
questions.hint: Ask what the resources would otherwise have produced, and where that figure would have been recorded.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The right to decide later
questions.learningObjective: explain what a real option is and what it is worth
questions.stem: Explain what a real option is in a decision, and give the sentence that treats the option as a bonus rather than a cost.

answer.exemplar: A real option is the right, bought by committing to nothing, to take a decision later when more will be known, and the cost of holding it is that the choice stays open only for a price, since waiting consumes the resources that the committed action would have started and may let a rival move first. That cost is what separates an option from a free benefit, and the value of the option is the best future decision's worth less the value of deciding now, which is positive only when the value of learning is large enough to pay for the delay. The sentence that treats the option as a bonus says the flexibility has no cost, since nothing has been spent yet, and the error is that the delay is not free: the plant not built is the plant not earning, and the option to expand is not the same thing as a decision to build. The useful discipline is to price the delay explicitly and to ask what the delay risks, because an option that expires on someone else's timetable is an option somebody else controls.

questions.explanation: The option is valuable precisely because it substitutes information for commitment, and it is expensive for the same reason, since the substitution is not free and the resources committed elsewhere while waiting are a real cost. A calculation that shows the option's value as pure upside has forgotten the premium, and one that prices the premium without the upside will reject every option and end up committing under uncertainty every time. Both figures are needed, along with the date the option expires, which is often set by a competitor rather than by physics.
questions.hint: Ask what waiting costs, and what it buys, and which of the two the calculation has left out.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Deciding now against deciding later
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes a delay worth paying for
questions.stem: Explain when waiting is the better decision even though acting now is worth more on paper, and give the sentence that would justify rushing instead.

answer.exemplar: Waiting is better when the decision can be unmade, because a decision that can be reversed at a known cost is worth less than a decision that can be reversed cheaply later, and the discount rate applied to the delayed pay-off is the price of the option to reverse rather than evidence that delay is unwise. The three things that have to be checked are the reversibility of the decision, what the delay reveals, and what the delay costs in the meantime, since a delay that reveals nothing and costs a year is never right. A decision that cannot be reversed is different in kind, because being wrong is permanent there, and it is that asymmetry, not a higher discount rate, that is the real cost of committing early. The sentence that would justify rushing says the paper numbers favour acting now, which is true of the cash flows and silent about the option value, and its error is treating the discount rate as a verdict on delay when in a reversible decision the rate is the price of waiting rather than a reason not to.

questions.explanation: The distinction between a reversible and an irreversible decision changes what a delay is worth, because a reversible one can be made twice and therefore benefits from what the first attempt revealed, while an irreversible one is made once whatever is learned afterwards. Getting that right is what stops the discount rate from being over-read, since a rate applied to a delayed pay-off is pricing the option to change your mind and not measuring the cost of indecision. The check that matters is whether the second decision is genuinely available, and a decision with a deadline set by a competitor is not reversible in any useful sense.
questions.hint: Ask whether the decision can be made again, and what the delay would reveal.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: From a forecast to a decision
questions.learningObjective: order the stages that turn a forecast into a defensible decision
questions.stem: A forecast is in hand and a decision has to be made. Put the four stages in the order that ends in a choice somebody can defend rather than one that feels right.

options.text: Name the states that can occur and the actions available, since both are needed before anything can be valued
Attach a probability to each state, written down so it can be disagreed with rather than assumed
Compute the expected value of each action and compare them against what each action costs
Check the alternatives and the reversibility, and record the decision with the assumptions it rests on

questions.explanation: The states and the actions come first because an expected value needs both, and a forecast that names no state cannot be turned into a number by any amount of arithmetic. The probabilities are written down next so that a reader can attack the weakest one, which is usually where the disagreement with a decision actually lies, and the expected values are compared against costs only after that, since a comparison of expected values with no cost in it will approve an action that loses money on average. The final check on alternatives and reversibility is what catches the decision that was never really a choice, and recording the assumptions is what makes the choice reviewable when the probabilities turn out to have been generous.
questions.hint: Ask what has to exist before a number can be computed, and which checks can overturn the arithmetic.
